Here are several proven strategies for reducing heating costs in an apartment building. You can combine measures to maximize savings:

1. Improve Insulation and Airtightness  
   • Wall and Roof Insulation – Upgrade to high-performance insulation materials (e.g., mineral wool, PIR panels) to lower heat losses through building envelope.  
   • Floor and Basement Insulation – Add rigid insulation under suspended floors or at the interface with unheated spaces.  
   • Seal Air Leaks – Use weather-stripping, window seals and foam sealants around doors, windows, service penetrations and ductwork to eliminate drafts.

2. Upgrade Windows and Doors  
   • High-performance Glazing – Replace single- or poorly insulated double-glazing with low-E, argon-filled triple-glazed units.  
   • Thermally Broken Frames – Choose frames with thermal breaks (e.g., fiberglass, PVC) to reduce conductive heat loss.

3. Modernize Heating System  
   • High-Efficiency Boilers or Heat Pumps – Swap older boilers (especially those >15 years old) for condensing boilers (efficiency >90 %) or ground/air-source heat pumps (seasonal COP 3–4+).  
   • Zoning and Smart Controls – Install programmable thermostats and thermostatic radiator valves so each apartment or floor can be heated according to occupancy and comfort needs.  
   • System Balancing – Have a qualified technician perform hydraulic balancing to ensure even heat distribution and avoid overheating some radiators while under-heating others.

4. Optimize Ventilation and Heat Recovery  
   • Controlled Mechanical Ventilation (CMV) – Upgrade to a balanced ventilation system with heat recovery (HRV/ERV). These systems recover up to 90 % of the heat from exhaust air.  
   • Regular Maintenance – Clean or replace filters and check fans to ensure the system runs at peak efficiency.

5. Metering and Resident Engagement  
   • Sub-Metering – Install individual heat- or energy-meters for each apartment so residents pay for what they consume. This typically drives behavioral changes and reduces waste.  
   • Information Campaigns – Educate residents about optimal thermostat settings (18–21 °C when home, lower when away/asleep) and simple habits (closing doors, reporting drafts).

6. Renewable and Low-Carbon Integration  
   • Solar Thermal or PV – Add solar collectors for hot-water preheating or photovoltaic panels to offset the building’s electricity use (pumps, fans, controls).  
   • District Heating – If available, connect to a modern district heating network, which often supplies heat more efficiently than individual boilers.

7. Regular Maintenance and Monitoring  
   • Annual Service – Have heating equipment serviced annually for combustion safety, burner calibration and filter changes.  
   • Energy Monitoring – Use a building-level energy management system (EMS) to track consumption in real time, spot anomalies and verify savings after upgrades.

By combining envelope improvements, system upgrades, smart controls and resident engagement, many apartment buildings can cut heating costs by 20 – 50 %—often amortizing their investment within 5–10 years through lower energy bills.

An energy declaration (in Sweden often called an energideklaration or EPC) is intended to give a building’s board a clear, standardized picture of the property’s current energy performance and where savings can be made. In practice it will include:

1. Energy class (epc_egienergiklass)  
   • A rating from A+ (best) to G showing how the building compares to national benchmarks.  

2. Annual energy use (kWh/m²·year)  
   • The building’s measured or calculated energy consumption per heated square metre, often broken down by heating, hot water, ventilation and any building‐specific systems.  

3. Heated floor area (Atemp) (epc_egenatemp)  
   • Total heated space in square metres, so consumption figures can be normalized and compared.  

4. Building description  
   • Type of building (epc_egenbyggnadstyp, e.g. detached house, multi‐family block), construction year and main construction materials.  
   • Number of above‐ground floors (epc_egenantalplan) and stairwells (epc_egenantaltrapphus).  

5. Technical system overview  
   • Information on heating plant, ventilation systems, cooling (if any) and domestic hot water installations.  

6. Recommendations for improvements  
   • A list of costed and prioritized energy‐saving measures (e.g. added insulation, window upgrades, system replacements), with estimated investment cost, annual energy savings and payback period.  

7. Indoor climate and CO₂ emissions  
   • Brief assessment of indoor thermal comfort and an estimate of the building’s carbon footprint.  

For a board, the EPC is primarily a decision‐support tool: it shows current performance, benchmarks it against similar buildings, and identifies the most cost‐effective steps for lowering energy use, reducing running costs and cutting emissions.

When the goal is to lower your building’s heating costs, the most effective approach is to first identify where you lose the most heat—and then tackle the improvements in order of greatest impact and lowest cost. Below is a recommended sequence of priorities:

1. Conduct an Energy Audit or Review Your EPC  
   • If you have an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC), note its energy class (A–G) and the biggest heat-loss items.  
   • A professional energy audit can pinpoint which measures will yield the best payback in your specific building.

2. Improve the Building Envelope  
   a. Loft or Roof Insulation  
      – Upgrading to at least 300–400 mm of mineral wool or equivalent high-performance insulation can cut heat losses through the roof by up to 30%.  
   b. External or Cavity Wall Insulation  
      – Injected or internal insulation of cavity walls, or external render systems, can reduce wall heat losses by 25–35%.  
   c. Floor and Basement Insulation  
      – Insulating between joists or adding rigid insulation under concrete slabs prevents ground-related heat loss.  
   d. Windows and Doors  
      – Replace single-glazed windows with modern double or triple-glazed units featuring low-e coatings.  
      – Upgrade door seals, thresholds and use insulated doors on exterior entrances.

3. Eliminate Drafts and Air Leaks  
   – Seal gaps around windows, doors, service penetrations and roof hatches with gaskets or expanding foam.  
   – Install controlled ventilation (see point 5) rather than relying on uncontrolled leaks.

4. Upgrade the Heating System  
   – Replace old, non-condensing boilers with A-rated condensing boilers or a ground/source heat pump.  
   – Ensure radiators are correctly sized and balanced; add thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) for room-by-room control.  
   – Consider adding buffer tanks or weather-compensation controls to reduce on/off cycling.

5. Install Mechanical Ventilation with Heat Recovery (MVHR)  
   – A balanced ventilation system with 70–90 % heat recovery captures heat from stale indoor air while ensuring good indoor air quality.  
   – This reduces the need for background heating to compensate for ventilation losses.

6. Smart Controls and Zoning  
   – Use programmable thermostats or smart controls to lower temperatures at night or when the building is unoccupied.  
   – Divide the building into heating zones so you only heat the areas in use.

7. Regular Maintenance and Monitoring  
   – Flush and power-flush heating circuits annually to maintain pump and heat‐exchanger efficiency.  
   – Check and bleed radiators, service boilers and controls each season.  
   – Install an energy-monitoring tool to track consumption trends and detect faults early.

8. Renewable and Supplementary Measures  
   – Solar thermal panels can pre-heat domestic hot water, reducing boiler runtime.  
   – Consider photovoltaic panels to offset electricity used by pumps and controls.  
   – Explore low-carbon district heating, where available.

By following this hierarchy—starting with the building envelope, then system efficiency and controls, and finally renewables—you’ll achieve the greatest reduction in heating energy demand and operating costs.

Since no specific data about your building’s current performance or use‐case was provided, here are generally applicable priorities you should consider, listed roughly in order of impact and regulatory importance:

1. Energy Efficiency and EPC Rating  
   • Obtain or review your latest Energy Performance Certificate (EPC), in particular the “epc_egienergiklass” (energy class).  
   • If you are in a lower band (D–G), target the most cost-effective measures first—improving insulation, sealing air leaks, and upgrading to high-performance windows.  
   • Next, look at your heating, cooling and ventilation systems: consider a modern heat pump, energy recovery ventilation (ERV) and more efficient boilers or controls.  

2. Indoor Climate and Occupant Health  
   • Ensure adequate ventilation rates to control humidity, CO₂ and other pollutants.  
   • Use low-emission materials (paints, sealants, flooring) to limit volatile organic compounds (VOCs).  
   • Monitor thermal comfort and daylight levels in occupied zones; poor comfort can lead to productivity losses or health complaints.  

3. Regulatory Compliance and Safety  
   • Verify compliance with local building codes for fire safety, accessibility (entrances, ramps, lifts) and structural requirements.  
   • Update fire alarms, emergency lighting and escape signage if these systems are older than 10 years or do not meet current standards.  

4. Lifecycle and Maintenance Planning  
   • Develop a rolling-stock plan for roof coverings, façades and critical MEP (Mechanical/Electrical/Plumbing) components.  
   • Prioritize components nearing the end of their service life to avoid unplanned failures and costly emergency repairs.  

5. Sustainability and Future-Proofing  
   • Investigate on-site renewables (solar PV panels, small wind turbines) or green electricity contracts to reduce carbon footprint.  
   • Design any major retrofit so it can accommodate future upgrades—e.g. space for battery storage or electric‐vehicle charging infrastructure.

By focusing first on improving your EPC energy class, you’ll reduce operating costs and environmental impact most dramatically. Once energy improvements are underway, shift attention to occupant health, safety and long-term maintenance to maximize comfort, compliance and asset value.

Direct-acting (also called direct-acting) electric radiators convert nearly 100 % of the electricity they consume into heat at the point of use. However, when assessing their overall energy efficiency and cost-effectiveness, you need to consider several factors:

1. Point-of-use efficiency  
   – Electric radiators themselves are “perfect” heaters in that all incoming electrical energy becomes heat in the room.  
   – There are no flue losses or standby heat losses through water pipes.  

2. Primary (well-to-room) efficiency  
   – If your electricity comes from fossil-fuel power plants, there are generation and transmission losses (typically 25–40 % losses before the electricity reaches your home).  
   – Even with modern combined-cycle gas or renewable sources, some losses occur upstream.  

3. Running costs  
   – Electricity per kWh is often more expensive than district heating, natural gas, or heat‐pump-supplied heat.  
   – Direct-acting electric radiators are therefore usually the most costly way to maintain a comfortable indoor temperature over long periods.  

4. Flexibility and installation  
   – Very simple to install and control (no water circuits, no pumps).  
   – Ideal for intermittent or supplemental heating (e.g., in a seldom-used room, garage or holiday home).  
   – Programmable thermostats and “smart” controls can optimize usage and reduce bills.  

5. Comparison with alternatives  
   – Air-to-air or ground-source heat pumps typically deliver 3–5 kWh of heat per kWh of electricity (COP 3–5), dramatically reducing running costs.  
   – District heating and modern biomass boilers can also be more economical if available.  

Recommendations  
– Use direct-acting electric radiators primarily for occasional or zoning purposes rather than whole-house heating.  
– Combine with time-of-use electricity tariffs, smart controls and good insulation to minimize operating hours and costs.  
– For full-time heating in a permanent residence, consider a heat-pump solution or another lower-cost heat source.

Here are several practical ways to get the most out of direct-acting electric radiators while keeping your costs and energy use down:

1. Use programmable or smart controls  
   • Fit each radiator with a digital thermostat or timer so it only runs when you need it (e.g. pre-heat living areas before you wake or return home).  
   • Lower the setpoint by a degree or two at night or when rooms are unoccupied—each °C you drop can cut energy use by around 5 %.

2. Zone your heating  
   • Only heat the rooms you’re actually using. Close doors to unused rooms and turn off their radiators.  
   • In larger homes, consider grouping radiators onto separate circuits so you can control whole zones simultaneously.

3. Take advantage of radiator-mounted thermostatic valves  
   • A TRV (thermostatic radiator valve) automatically maintains the temperature you choose within each room, preventing overheating.  
   • If you don’t have TRVs, look for a model designed for retrofit—installation is usually straightforward.

4. Improve heat retention in the room  
   • Ensure windows, doors and any through-wall vents are well sealed and draught-proofed.  
   • Add heavy curtains or blinds over windows and close them at dusk.  
   • Install reflective foil behind radiators on external walls to push heat back into the living space.

5. Optimise radiator placement and airflow  
   • Keep radiators clear of furniture, curtains or anything else that blocks airflow.  
   • Position furniture to encourage warm air to circulate rather than trapping it in one spot.

6. Run radiators in “eco” or low-power mode where available  
   • Many modern electric heaters offer an “eco” or “low” mode that cycles the element on and off to save energy while still maintaining comfort.  
   • Experiment with these settings to find a balance between comfort and cost.

7. Monitor and adjust regularly  
   • Keep an eye on your electricity meter or smart-meter app so you can see how changes in settings affect consumption.  
   • Tweak schedules or setpoints as the seasons change—your summer-to-autumn needs will differ from deep winter.

8. Consider supplementary insulation upgrades  
   • While not a radiator tweak per se, improving loft insulation, cavity-wall insulation or even under-floor insulation reduces the workload on your heaters and can be highly cost-effective.

By combining good controls, proper maintenance and attention to heat loss, you’ll keep each direct-acting electric radiator running as efficiently as possible—and avoid paying to heat the great outdoors.

Improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot‐water (DHW) systems typically involves reducing both the energy required to heat the water and the losses that occur between generation and end‐use.  The following measures are among the most effective:

1. Improve Generation Efficiency  
   • Upgrade to a high-efficiency water heater or boiler (e.g., condensing gas boiler or electric heat-pump water heater).  
   • Consider on-demand (tankless) water heaters in smaller households — they eliminate standby losses entirely.  
   • If feasible, integrate solar thermal collectors or a solar-assisted heat-pump to preheat the incoming cold water.

2. Reduce Distribution and Storage Losses  
   • Insulate hot-water storage tanks with at least 75 mm (3 in) of high-density foam or mineral-wool insulation.  
   • Insulate all hot-water piping (including any return lines) to minimize conductive heat loss.  
   • Install point-of-use mini-tanks in remote bathrooms or kitchens so that water does not sit unused in long runs of pipe.  
   • If your system uses a recirculation loop, fit it with a timer or a demand-controlled relay (motion sensor or push-button) so that hot water only circulates when needed.

3. Lower Temperature Set-Points  
   • Reduce the thermostat on your water heater to around 55–60 °C (130–140 °F) — this is usually sufficient for hygiene and comfort while cutting standby heat loss.  
   • Install a thermostatic mixing valve at fixtures to deliver water at a safe, lower end-use temperature and avoid scalding.

4. Minimize Consumption  
   • Fit low-flow aerators and showerheads (6–8 l/min) to reduce hot-water demand without sacrificing user comfort.  
   • Repair any drips or leaks promptly to eliminate waste.  
   • Educate occupants on efficient behaviours (e.g., shorter showers, full-load dishwashing).

5. System Maintenance and Controls  
   • Flush and de-scale tanks and heat exchangers annually to maintain heat-transfer efficiency.  
   • Check sacrificial anode rods in storage tanks and replace them when depleted to protect against corrosion.  
   • Install accurately calibrated thermostats, timers or smart controls that optimize DHW production with occupancy patterns and utility‐rate schedules.

6. Heat Recovery Opportunities  
   • Recover heat from waste sources (e.g., greywater drain heat exchangers under showers).  
   • Use ventilation heat-recovery units capable of transferring exhaust‐air heat to preheat incoming cold water (via a plate or coil heat exchanger).

By combining improved generation technologies, better insulation, smart controls and reduced consumption, you can cut the energy required for domestic hot water by 20–50 percent or more, depending on your starting point.

Optimizing domestic hot‐water production in an apartment building involves improving the efficiency of generation, storage, distribution and control. Below are key strategies to consider:

1. Efficient Heat Generation  
  • Condensing boilers or high-efficiency heat pumps: These can achieve seasonal efficiencies above 90 %.  
  • District heating with plate‐type heat exchangers: If a district-heating network is available, a well-sized exchanger minimizes losses.  
  • Solar thermal pre-heating: Integrate a solar collector array to supply a significant share of the annual domestic hot-water (DHW) load.

2. Optimized Storage and Buffering  
  • Stratified storage tanks: Use tanks with internal baffles or heat‐exchanger coils to maintain a high “top‐layer” temperature while reducing recirculation losses.  
  • Correct sizing: Oversized tanks increase standby losses, undersized tanks lead to frequent boiler cycling. Aim for about 25–35 L of storage per apartment.  
  • Thermal insulation: Insulate all tanks (≥ 100 mm of mineral wool or equivalent) to reduce heat losses.

3. Minimizing Distribution Losses  
  • Pipe insulation: Wrap all hot‐water pipes with at least 25–50 mm of closed-cell insulation.  
  • Recirculation loops with smart controls: Install a low-energy circulator pump with temperature sensors or timers to avoid running the pump continuously.  
  • Zoning: Divide the building into vertical or horizontal zones so that the recirculation loop serves only a portion of the apartments, further reducing return‐line losses.

4. Advanced Control and Monitoring  
  • Demand‐controlled circulation: Use flow‐sensors or temperature differentials to switch the recirculation pump on only when there is actual draw or significant temperature drop.  
  • Thermostatic mixing valves at distribution manifolds: Keep supply temperature high (e.g. 60 °C) to prevent legionella, then mix down to a safe delivery temperature (≈ 50 °C) at the apartment.  
  • Sub‐metering and data logging: Install energy meters on each riser or at individual apartments to track consumption and identify faults or leaks.

5. Preventive Maintenance  
  • Regular descaling and cleaning: Hard-water areas may require periodic flushing of heat-exchanger surfaces and boiler internals.  
  • Legionella control: Maintain dead‐leg flushing schedules and check tank and loop temperatures monthly.  
  • Pump and valve checks: Verify that balancing valves, check valves and thermostatic valves are functioning and properly adjusted.

6. Renewable and Hybrid Integration  
  • Solar thermal with auxiliary backup: A well-designed solar system can cover 30–50 % of annual DHW needs, with gas or electric backup.  
  • Heat‐pump booster for recirculation loops: Small decentralized heat pumps can raise return-loop temperature, improving overall system COP.  
  • Photovoltaic‐driven instant‐electric heaters: In some layouts, PV panels can power point‐of-use electric heaters to cover peak morning draw.

7. User Engagement and Behavioral Measures  
  • Low‐flow fixtures: Install aerators or pressure-compensating mixers (6–8 L/min) to reduce water and energy use.  
  • Resident information: Provide guidelines on sensible temperature settings (e.g. 50 °C at tap) and short shower times.  
  • Feedback displays: Smart thermo-meters in each apartment encourage residents to monitor and reduce consumption.

By combining high-efficiency generation, well-insulated storage, intelligent circulation control, regular maintenance and user engagement, you can reduce heat losses, minimize cycling, and deliver hot water more sustainably and cost-effectively throughout the apartment building.

An energy declaration (often called an Energy Performance Certificate or EPC) is an official, standardized report that describes a building’s energy performance and efficiency. In Sweden, for example, any newly constructed, sold or rented building must have an energideklaration performed by an accredited energy inspector. Key elements of the declaration include:  
• An energy class rating (epc_egienergiklass) on a scale from A (most efficient) to G (least efficient)  
• Estimated annual energy consumption for heating, hot water and, where relevant, electricity for common areas  
• Technical building data such as heated floor area (Atemp), building type, number of floors and stairwells  
• A list of recommended energy-saving measures with cost and energy-saving estimates  
• Validity period (typically ten years)  

The purpose of the energy declaration is to give building owners, buyers and tenants clear, comparable information on a building’s energy use and to highlight cost-effective ways to reduce consumption, lower operating costs and improve indoor comfort.

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any change—whether in design, equipment, operation or occupant behavior—that reduces a building’s energy consumption while delivering the same level of service (heating, cooling, lighting, hot water, ventilation, etc.). In practice, it covers a wide range of measures, for example:  
• Building envelope upgrades – adding or improving insulation, installing low-U-value windows, sealing air leaks around doors and windows  
• HVAC system modernization – replacing old boilers, furnaces or air-conditioning units with high-efficiency models; installing appropriately sized heat pumps  
• Ventilation and heat-recovery – fitting balanced ventilation systems with heat-recovery units to retain indoor warmth while maintaining air quality  
• Lighting and controls – switching to LED lighting, daylight-responsive or occupancy sensors, and advanced building-management systems  
• Appliance and system optimization – choosing energy-efficient domestic appliances, upgrading pumps and motors, and tuning control algorithms  
• Behavior and operation – educating occupants in energy-saving practices, optimizing setback schedules, and performing regular maintenance  

Key benefits of energy-efficiency improvements include lower energy bills, reduced greenhouse-gas emissions, improved indoor comfort, and often an enhanced EPC (Energy Performance Certificate) rating or energy class. Success is typically measured by comparing annual energy use (kWh/m²) or by tracking percentage reductions in energy consumption against a defined baseline.

In any building, you will typically find a mix of different “premises” or room-types, each of which has its own impact on the property’s overall energy use. Below is an overview of the most common categories and how they influence energy consumption:

1. Residential Premises  
   • Examples: apartments, single-family rooms, bedrooms, living rooms.  
   • Energy impact:  
     – Space heating and cooling dominate (set‐point temperature, hours of occupancy).  
     – Domestic hot water (showers, kitchens) can be a significant share.  
     – Internal heat gains from appliances and occupants can reduce heating demand in winter but increase cooling demand in summer.

2. Commercial Premises  
   • Examples: offices, retail areas, restaurants, hotels.  
   • Energy impact:  
     – Often have long operating hours (early morning to late evening), driving up lighting, HVAC and plug‐load energy.  
     – Higher lighting power density and more intensive ventilation requirements (fresh-air rates per person).  
     – Kitchens and catering areas are particularly energy-intensive (cooking equipment, ventilation hoods).

3. Industrial Premises  
   • Examples: factories, workshops, process halls.  
   • Energy impact:  
     – Process machinery and equipment often require large amounts of electricity or process steam.  
     – Specialized ventilation (dust extraction, temperature-control) can be a major component.  
     – Often less focus on space heating for production halls but significant energy for processes.

4. Technical/Plant Rooms  
   • Examples: boiler rooms, pump rooms, electrical switchgear rooms.  
   • Energy impact:  
     – Usually heated to a low level year-round to protect equipment from freezing, but overall area is small.  
     – Continuous operation of pumps, fans and controls adds a steady electrical load.

5. Storage Premises  
   • Examples: unheated warehouses, cellars, lofts.  
   • Energy impact:  
     – If unheated, they contribute very little to the building’s space‐heating energy.  
     – Temperature-sensitive storage (food, pharmaceuticals) may require refrigeration or heating.

6. Parking and Garage Areas  
   • Examples: indoor parking, carports, bicycle storage.  
   • Energy impact:  
     – Often unheated or only frost-protected; heating demand is minimal.  
     – Lighting and ventilation are the main electrical loads.

7. Common Areas and Circulation Spaces  
   • Examples: stairwells, corridors, lobbies, elevator shafts.  
   • Energy impact:  
     – Typically heated to a lower set-point than dwelling units.  
     – Lighting controlled by motion sensors can reduce electricity use, but high traffic means frequent illumination.

How They Affect the Building’s Energy Performance Certificate (EPC)  
– The EPC aggregates all heated areas (Atemp) to calculate space-heating demand.  
– Areas that are unheated or frost-protected are excluded from the primary heating load but still appear in the certificate if they use electricity or ventilation.  
– High-use commercial or industrial processes show up primarily in the building’s total delivered energy (kWh/m²), pushing the EPC to a lower (worse) energy class.  
– Conversely, large unheated storage or parking areas dilute the total heated area, which can improve the apparent energy performance per square meter of heated floor space.

In practice, the more you can tailor heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting to the actual use-patterns of each type of premises (for example through zoning, time-based controls and efficient equipment), the better the building’s overall energy performance—and the higher its EPC energy class will be.

In multi-unit buildings the common-area electricity load typically breaks down into the following main categories:

1. Lighting  
   – General illumination of corridors, stairwells and lobbies (often switched via corridors’ light switches or time clocks)  
   – Emergency and escape-route lighting (centrally monitored and on battery backup)  
   – Decorative or accent lighting in entrance foyers  

2. Vertical transport  
   – Lift motors, drives and control electronics  
   – Lift-shaft lighting and ventilation fans  

3. Controls and auxiliary systems  
   – Motion, presence or daylight sensors that switch lights on/off automatically  
   – Door-opening mechanisms (automatic sliding or swing doors)  
   – Access-control readers and intercoms  

4. Ventilation, heating and cooling  
   – Fan coils or AHU (air-handling units) in lobbies and stairwells to maintain minimum ventilation rates  
   – Electric heaters (where installed for frost-protection in stairwells)  

5. Safety and communications  
   – Fire-alarm panels, smoke extractors and alarm sounders  
   – CCTV cameras, card-readers or door-entry telephone panels  

By switching to LED luminaires, installing presence detectors and using central building-management system (BMS) scheduling, many properties significantly reduce their common-area electricity consumption without compromising comfort or safety.

In multi‐family residential buildings (apartment blocks), the energy performance certificate (EPC/Energideklaration) typically identifies a range of cost‐effective measures. The most common energy‐efficiency upgrades include:

•  Building‐envelope insulation  
  – Cavity‐wall and external‐wall insulation  
  – Loft (roof) and floor insulation (especially over unheated spaces)  
  – Sealing of thermal bridges and reduction of air leakage (draught‐proofing)

•  High-performance windows and doors  
  – Replacement of single‐ or old double-glazed units with modern low-emissivity (low-E) triple or double glazing  
  – Improved frame materials (e.g. thermally broken aluminum or wood‐composite frames)  
  – Proper sealing and weatherstripping

•  Upgrades to heating and hot-water systems  
  – Conversion from old boilers to condensing boilers or district heating connection  
  – Installation of ground‐source or air-source heat pumps  
  – Tank insulation and heat‐recovery from hot‐water circulation loops  
  – Thermostatic radiator valves or electronic room thermostats in each apartment

•  Ventilation and indoor-air quality improvements  
  – Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR, FTX units)  
  – Demand-controlled ventilation (CO₂ or humidity sensors)  
  – Balancing of ductwork to optimise airflow

•  Lighting and controls  
  – Replacement of fluorescent or incandescent lamps with LED fixtures  
  – Presence detectors and daylight dimming controls in common areas  
  – Centralised lighting control systems for corridors, stairwells and underground parking

•  Building automation and energy management  
  – Installation of building-management systems (BMS) that monitor and adjust heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting  
  – Sub-metering of electricity, heat and hot water per staircase or individual flats to encourage resident engagement  
  – Remote monitoring and fault detection

•  Renewable‐energy integration  
  – Photovoltaic (PV) panels on roofs or façades for on-site electricity production  
  – Solar‐thermal collectors for domestic hot‐water pre-heating  
  – Shared battery storage or vehicle-to-grid integration in emerging projects

•  Water‐saving and waste‐heat recovery  
  – Low-flow taps, showerheads and dual-flush toilets to reduce hot‐water demand  
  – Heat recovery from grey-water (showers, sinks) in large complexes  
  – Centralised laundry facilities with heat-recovery dryers

Most EPCs will prioritise measures according to cost-effectiveness, expected energy savings (kWh/m², kWh/person) and pay-back time. In most residential and smaller commercial buildings, electricity consumption can be grouped into five to seven broad end-use categories. Although the exact shares will vary from one property to another (depending on climate, building systems, occupant behaviour and fuel mix), the following uses are almost always the largest:

1. Space heating (when electric heating is installed)  
   • Often the single biggest electricity demand – in an all-electric home it can account for 40–50 % (or more) of total consumption.  
   • Includes resistance radiators, heat pumps (compressor power), underfloor electric mats, fan coil units, etc.

2. Domestic hot water  
   • Typically 10–20 % of electricity use in an electrically heated building.  
   • Covers storage-tank immersion heaters, instantaneous electric water heaters and heat‐pump water heaters.

3. Ventilation, cooling and pumps  
   • Mechanical ventilation fans, air-conditioning compressors, circulation pumps for heat distribution, pool pumps, etc.  
   • Depending on climate and system efficiency, this can be 10–20 % (higher in warmer climates or poorly insulated buildings).

4. Household appliances (“white goods”)  
   • Refrigerators, freezers, washing machines, dishwashers, tumble dryers, and similar.  
   • Typically 10–15 % in an electric-heated house, but larger if the dwelling is very appliance-intensive or lacks other electrical heating loads.

5. Lighting  
   • Interior and exterior lighting (including security and landscape lighting).  
   • In a modern, LED-lit home you might see 5–10 %; in an older building with incandescent or fluorescent fittings it can be 15 % or more.

6. Cooking and built-in kitchen equipment  
   • Electric ranges, ovens, hobs, microwaves and extractor fans.  
   • Usually 5–10 % of total electricity, though higher in homes where electric cooking is predominant.

7. Small electronics and miscellaneous loads  
   • TVs, computers, chargers, entertainment systems, smart-home devices, standby losses, etc.  
   • Generally 5–15 %, but rising as more devices and “always-on” equipment are installed.

Key drivers of variation  
• If the building uses district heating or gas for space and water heating, the electricity share for heating drops to nearly zero and lighting/appliances/electronics dominate.  
• Highly efficient heat pumps can reduce the electricity share for space and water heating, shifting the balance toward appliances and lighting.  
• In commercial or office buildings, lighting, HVAC (ventilation and cooling), and ICT (servers, computers) often dominate.

In summary, while “space heating” (in electrically heated properties), “domestic hot water” and “ventilation/cooling” are the largest single buckets in many all-electric buildings, appliances, lighting and small electronics together typically account for at least 30–40 % of the annual electricity demand in most homes.

Natural (or passive) ventilation relies on wind pressure and thermal buoyancy to move air through a building, whereas mechanical ventilation uses fans and ductwork. Compared with mechanical systems, natural ventilation offers several key advantages:

1. Lower Energy Use and Operating Costs  
   • No or very low fan-power requirements, so you save on electricity.  
   • Eliminates ongoing HVAC-related operating expenses.  

2. Reduced Carbon Footprint  
   • Fewer moving parts and no continuous fan operation mean less greenhouse-gas emissions from power plants.  

3. Simplified Installation and Maintenance  
   • Fewer mechanical components (no fans, motors or complex controls) reduce upfront equipment costs.  
   • Lower maintenance burden—no regular filter replacements or fan inspections.

4. Improved Indoor Air Quality and Comfort  
   • Fresh outdoor air supply can feel more “natural,” reducing perceptions of stuffiness.  
   • Automatic variation in airflow can create a more dynamic, comfortable environment.

5. Enhanced Occupant Well-Being  
   • Direct connection to outdoor conditions (breezes, fresh air) can improve mood, concentration and productivity.  
   • Opportunities for daylighting and views often coincide with operable windows.

6. Resilience and Reliability  
   • Passive systems continue to function during power outages or mechanical failures.  
   • Less vulnerability to breakdowns, power surges or equipment obsolescence.

7. Noise Reduction (in Some Cases)  
   • Absence of fan noise can make for a quieter interior—although wind-driven noise at open windows should be considered.

When designing for natural ventilation, it’s important to carefully consider climate, building orientation, window placement and internal layouts to ensure adequate airflow and avoid issues such as drafts, overheating or security concerns. In many projects, a hybrid approach—combining natural and mechanical ventilation—yields the best balance of energy performance, comfort and flexibility.

Optimizing natural ventilation in a house boils down to encouraging airflow through well-placed openings, taking advantage of wind pressure and thermal buoyancy, and controlling solar gains. Below are key strategies:

1. Orientation and Openings  
   • Place operable windows or vents on opposite facades (or diagonal corners) to establish a clear cross-ventilation path.  
   • In wind-dominated climates, ensure one side faces prevailing winds (windward) and the opposite side provides an easy exhaust (leeward).  

2. Stack (Buoyancy) Ventilation  
   • Incorporate high-level openings—clerestory windows, roof vents or a “solar chimney”—to let warm air escape at ceiling/roof level.  
   • Pair these with low-level inlets (e.g. trickle vents, under-window grilles) so cooler outdoor air is drawn in at floor level.  

3. Window and Vent Design  
   • Use top-hung or louvre‐type vents to catch airflow from different angles without compromising security or rain protection.  
   • Provide adjustable vents above internal doors or in partition walls to allow airflow even when doors are closed.  

4. Architectural Features  
   • Introduce atria, light wells or internal courtyards that act as vertical chimneys, enhancing stack effect.  
   • Fit wind catchers (“malqaf”) or roof-mounted wind scoops in locations with consistent wind.  

5. Solar Shading and Thermal Mass  
   • Minimize unwanted heat gain by shading windows with overhangs, fins or external shutters—this reduces indoor overheating that can actually stall buoyancy‐driven flows.  
   • Use thermal-mass elements (exposed concrete or brick) to store cool night air and release it slowly, smoothing temperature swings.  

6. Seasonal and Occupant Control  
   • In summer evenings, fully open low-level windows after sunset to “flush” stored heat out. Close them and lower blinds at sunrise to trap coolness.  
   • In colder weather, keep high vents partly open to maintain air quality without excessive heat loss; use trickle vents rather than fully open windows.  

7. Maintenance and Fine-Tuning  
   • Keep vents and window tracks clean and lubricated to ensure they open fully.  
   • Install simple airflow indicators (e.g. smoke tubes) to verify that your cross‐ and stack‐drives are working as intended.  

By combining cross-ventilation (pressure differential), stack-ventilation (thermal differential) and careful solar management, you can achieve comfortable indoor climate without—or with minimal—mechanical cooling or ventilation.

When you’re evaluating whether to invest in solar panels, it’s important to look at a combination of technical, financial and regulatory factors. Here’s a detailed checklist to guide your decision:

1. Roof or Site Suitability  
   • Orientation and Tilt – South-facing roofs in the northern hemisphere (north in the southern hemisphere) with a pitch of 15–40° capture sunlight most efficiently.  
   • Shading – Even small amounts of shade from trees, chimneys or adjacent buildings can significantly reduce output.  
   • Structural Condition – Have a qualified roofer or engineer confirm that your roof can bear the extra weight and that it has sufficient remaining service life.

2. Energy Usage and System Sizing  
   • Current Consumption – Review your electricity bills for at least 12 months to establish your household or business’s typical usage pattern.  
   • Desired Offset – Decide whether you want to cover 100% of your load, a portion of it, or simply shave peak-hour costs.  
   • Future Changes – Account for potential increases in consumption (e.g., electric vehicles, heat pumps).

3. Equipment Choice  
   • Panel Type – Monocrystalline panels typically offer higher efficiency; polycrystalline can be lower-cost but slightly less efficient.  
   • Inverter Selection – String inverters are cost-effective; micro-inverters or power optimizers can improve performance under partial shading.  
   • Warranties and Certifications – Look for panels with at least a 10- to 25-year performance warranty and inverters with 5- to 10-year warranties. Ensure compliance with local or international standards (e.g., IEC 61215, UL 1703).

4. Financial Analysis  
   • Upfront Costs – Include panels, inverters, mounting hardware, labor, permit fees and any required electrical upgrades.  
   • Incentives and Subsidies – Research national or regional grants, tax credits, feed-in tariffs or net-metering arrangements that reduce net cost or improve payback.  
   • Payback Period and ROI – Estimate the system’s annual energy yield in kWh, multiply by your local electricity rate, subtract any ongoing maintenance costs, then calculate how many years to recoup your investment.

5. Regulatory and Grid-Connection Requirements  
   • Building Permits – Check with your municipality for required planning approvals or building permits.  
   • Grid-Tie Agreements – If you plan to export surplus power, you’ll need to arrange a connection agreement with your utility and possibly install a bi-directional meter.  
   • Safety and Inspections – Some jurisdictions require a final inspection or commissioning report before you can activate the system.

6. Installation and Maintenance  
   • Installer Qualifications – Choose an installer certified by a recognized body (for example, SEK or other accredited bodies in your country).  
   • Maintenance Plan – Solar systems are low-maintenance but benefits from periodic cleaning (especially in dusty areas), visual inspections of mounts and wiring checks every few years.  
   • Monitoring – Consider a monitoring platform (often provided by the inverter manufacturer) to track production, detect faults early and optimize performance.

7. Long-Term Considerations  
   • Degradation Rate – Panels lose a small percentage of efficiency each year (typically 0.5–0.8% per year).  
   • Battery Storage (Optional) – Adding batteries can increase self-consumption and provide backup power, but will raise upfront costs and complexity.  
   • Resale Value and Insurance – A well-installed solar system can enhance property value. Inform your insurer about the installation to ensure proper coverage.

By carefully assessing each of these areas, you can design a solar installation that matches your energy needs, budget and long-term goals—and maximize both environmental and financial returns.

The energy class of a building (often reported on its Energy Performance Certificate, or EPC, as “epc_egienergiklass”) is an overall indicator of how much energy the building envelope and its fixed systems (heating, ventilation, cooling, lighting) consume per square meter. When you know a building’s energy class, you can more effectively target where to save energy—and that in turn influences which household appliances will give you the best returns in reduced energy use and cost.  

1. Understanding the share of energy use  
   • In a high-performance building (e.g. energy class A or B), losses through walls, roof and windows are already low. As a result, appliances (white goods, electronics, cooking equipment) often become the single largest remaining energy draw. Investing in top-rated appliances (EU label A or B under the new A–G scale) will therefore yield relatively large percentage savings on total household consumption.  
   • In a lower-performance building (e.g. class D, E or lower), heating (and cooling, where relevant) typically dominates energy use. Although upgrading to efficient appliances still saves energy, the relative impact on your overall bill is smaller compared with fixing insulation, windows or heating systems first.  

2. Choosing appliance energy classes to match building performance  
   • If your building is rated A–B:  
     – Prioritize appliances in the top energy classes (A or B under the current EU A–G label).  
     – Look for models with features like inverter compressors (in refrigerators), “eco” wash cycles (in dishwashers and washing machines) and high SCOP/SEER values (in heat-pump water heaters or integrated heat-pump systems).  
   • If your building is rated C–D:  
     – A balance of mid-range appliances (class C or D) can be cost-effective if the purchase price premium for top-class units is very high.  
     – However, if you plan major building envelope upgrades in the near future, it can still make sense to choose top-class appliances up front so they operate efficiently once the building is improved.  
   • If your building is rated E–G:  
     – Focus first on building improvements (insulation, sealing, heating).  
     – In parallel, replacing very old appliances (classes F, G or un-labeled) with at least class C–D models will still produce noticeable savings and lower peaks on your existing heating system.  

3. Smart and integrated controls  
   No matter the building class, selecting appliances with smart-energy management functions can further reduce consumption. Features to look for include:  
   – Time-of-use programming (runs dishwashers, washing machines or charging stations when electricity is cheapest or when on-site renewables are producing).  
   – Load-shifting capabilities that coordinate with your home energy management system to avoid simultaneous high-power draws.  

4. Total cost of ownership  
   While high-class appliances often have a higher upfront cost, their lower electricity and water consumption usually pays back over the appliance’s lifetime—especially in a well-insulated, efficient building where heating costs are already minimized.  

Summary  
By aligning your choice of household appliances with the building’s EPC energy class, you ensure that your investment in efficiency yields the greatest possible savings. In a top-class building, appliances become the principal lever for further energy reduction. In a lower-class building, appliance upgrades are still beneficial but should be paired with improvements to the building envelope and fixed systems to maximize overall gains.

When shopping for a new refrigerator or freezer, look beyond size and style and focus on features that drive down energy consumption—both to reduce your utility bills and to lessen environmental impact. Key energy-saving features include:  

1. High Energy-Efficiency Rating  
   • In Europe: look for A +, A ++ or A +++ on the EU energy label (with A +++ being the most efficient).  
   • In the U.S.: choose ENERGY STAR–certified models.  
   • Compare the annual kWh consumption on the label—smaller numbers mean lower running costs.  

2. Inverter (Variable-Speed) Compressor  
   • Runs more smoothly and only as fast as needed, avoiding the constant on/off cycling of traditional compressors.  
   • Provides more precise temperature control, uses up to 20–30 % less energy and tends to be quieter.  

3. Efficient Insulation and Sealing  
   • Thick, high-density polyurethane foam in the walls and door.  
   • Magnetic door gaskets that form an airtight seal—inspect for uniform closure around the entire door.  
   • Automatic door-close or door-alarm features to prevent energy loss from accidentally propped-open doors.  

4. Frost-Free (Auto-Defrost) System  
   • Prevents ice build-up on evaporator coils, which otherwise forces the compressor to work harder.  
   • Maintains consistent cooling and reduces manual defrosting, saving both time and energy.  

5. LED Interior Lighting  
   • Uses significantly less electricity than incandescent or halogen bulbs and generates less heat (so the compressor doesn’t have to work as hard).  
   • Often longer-lasting, reducing maintenance and replacement costs.  

6. Precise Digital Temperature Controls  
   • Allows you to fine-tune temperatures in both fridge and freezer compartments to the ideal range (fridge: 3–5 °C; freezer: –18 °C).  
   • Built-in sensors and displays help prevent overcooling (which wastes energy) or undercooling (which can spoil food).  

7. Eco-Modes and Vacation Settings  
   • “Eco” or “Energy Saver” modes adjust defrost cycles and compressor run times to reduce consumption during periods of light use.  
   • “Vacation” or “Holiday” settings raise the fridge temperature slightly when you’re away but keep it above safety thresholds.  

8. Smart and Connectivity Features (Optional)  
   • Some models can monitor door openings, ambient temperature and energy consumption via a smartphone app.  
   • Alerts if the door is left ajar or if a power outage occurs—helping you prevent wasted energy and spoiled food.  

9. Right-Sizing and Configuration  
   • Choose the capacity you actually need; oversized units waste energy cooling dead space.  
   • A freezer compartment inside the fridge door or a small “mini-freezer” drawer can be more efficient than a two-door design if you only freeze a little.  

10. Placement and Installation Tips  
   • Allow proper ventilation around the back and sides—crowded or wall-pressed units must run longer.  
   • Keep your appliance out of direct sunlight or next to heat-emitting equipment (oven, radiator), which forces it to consume more energy.  

By prioritizing these features—especially a high energy-efficiency rating, inverter compressor technology, strong insulation with airtight seals, frost-free operation and LED lighting—you’ll secure a fridge or freezer that keeps your food cold while keeping energy use (and costs) to a minimum.

In most countries (including Sweden), you need two separate agreements to get power into your home or business: a grid (network) contract and an electricity supply contract. They cover different services and are made with different companies.  

1. Grid Contract (Nätavtal)  
   • Counterparty: your local grid or distribution system operator (DSO) – the company that owns and maintains the poles, wires and transformers in your area.  
   • Purpose: grants you a physical connection to the electrical network and ensures safe delivery of power.  
   • Charges:  
     – A fixed monthly fee or capacity fee for your contracted load (kW) or service level.  
     – A variable network fee based on how much electricity you draw (kWh).  
   • You cannot opt out of a grid contract if you want electricity—you must have one to receive any power.  

2. Electricity Supply Contract (Elhandelsavtal)  
   • Counterparty: an electricity retailer or supplier—often a different company than the DSO.  
   • Purpose: covers the purchase of the energy itself (the kWh you consume). You choose the supplier, price model and contract length.  
   • Common price models:  
     – Fixed‐price contract: you pay the same kWh price for the entire contract period.  
     – Variable/spot‐price contract: your price follows the hourly or daily market (Nord Pool) price plus a supplier margin.  
     – Mix or indexed contracts combining elements of both.  
   • You can switch suppliers (and thus your supply contract) without changing your physical connection or grid contract.  

Key takeaway  
• The grid contract ensures your building is connected to and serviced by the electrical network—its fees cover infrastructure and delivery.  
• The supply contract covers the commodity (electricity) you actually consume.  
You need both agreements in place: one to get power to your meter, the other to pay for the power you use.

Control and regulation technology (sometimes called automation or “styr- och reglerteknik” in Swedish) is the branch of engineering and applied science concerned with measuring, monitoring and automatically adjusting the behaviour of technical systems. In the context of building services and energy performance, it covers:

1. Sensors and Measurement  
   • Temperature, humidity, pressure, flow and light sensors  
   • Energy meters for electricity, gas or district heating  

2. Controllers and Logic  
   • Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) or building-automation controllers  
   • Control algorithms (e.g. PID-controllers) that compare measured values against set-points  

3. Actuators and Final Control Elements  
   • Valves, dampers, pumps and fans that respond to control signals  
   • Variable-speed drives and motor controllers  

4. Feedback and Regulation Loops  
   • Closed-loop control where the system continuously adjusts to maintain a desired condition (for example, keeping room temperature at 21 °C)  
   • Cascaded or multivariable loops for more complex processes (e.g. combined heating and ventilation control)  

5. Supervision and Integration  
   • Building Management Systems (BMS) or SCADA platforms that collect data, visualize system status and allow centralized commissioning, alarms and trend analysis  
   • Communication protocols such as BACnet, Modbus or KNX for interoperability  

Key benefits in buildings include:
– Energy efficiency through optimized operation of HVAC, lighting and other services  
– Improved occupant comfort and indoor environmental quality  
– Remote monitoring, fault detection and preventive maintenance  

In short, control and regulation technology is the toolbox—both hardware and software—that ensures technical systems operate safely, efficiently and in accordance with user requirements.

Expanding a control system generally involves three parallel tracks — instrumentation, hardware infrastructure and software/configuration:

1. Instrumentation  
   • Add new sensors (e.g. temperature, pressure, flow) and actuators (valves, dampers, motors) at the field level  
   • Ensure each device has the correct signal type (analog, digital, bus) and meets your accuracy or speed requirements  

2. Hardware and I/O  
   • If your main PLC or DCS chassis is full, install remote I/O racks or I/O extension modules on existing fieldbuses (Profibus, Modbus, EtherNet/IP, etc.)  
   • For larger systems, consider adding a second controller and architecting a distributed control topology  
   • Upgrade network switches or fieldbus segments to handle extra traffic, taking care to maintain proper segmentation and redundancy  

3. Software/Configuration  
   • In your PLC/DCS software, define the new I/O points, assign addresses/tags and incorporate them into your control logic  
   • Extend HMI/SCADA screens with new operator graphics, alarms and trends for the added loops  
   • Update alarm management and interlock matrices to include the new signals  
   • Run a full test plan (factory acceptance if possible, then on-site commissioning) to validate I/O wiring, control sequences and safety interlocks  

Additional considerations:  
• Documentation — update wiring diagrams, I/O lists, network drawings and control narratives  
• Cybersecurity — ensure any new network nodes adhere to your firewall/VLAN policies and security standards  
• Licensing — verify that you have sufficient PLC/DCS and SCADA software licenses for the extra tags  
• Future-proofing — if you anticipate further growth, leave some chassis or network capacity in reserve  

By carefully planning instrumentation additions, augmenting I/O hardware and methodically extending your control logic and operator interfaces, you can scale your control system in a structured, reliable way.

Load balancing in the context of electric-vehicle (EV) charging is a method for distributing available electrical power among one or more charging points so that you never exceed the capacity of your supply (meter, transformer or local grid connection). It enables you to install multiple chargers—even on a relatively modest mains connection—without tripping breakers or incurring costly network upgrades.  

Key aspects of EV-charging load balancing  

1. Why it’s needed  
   • Prevents overloads – A typical household or commercial supply can only deliver a certain maximum current. If two or more chargers draw their full power simultaneously, you risk exceeding that limit.  
   • Cost savings – By avoiding network-operator connection upgrades or higher demand charges, you keep capital and operating costs down.  
   • Grid friendliness – Helps flatten peaks in electricity consumption, easing stress on local transformers and the wider distribution network.  

2. Static vs. Dynamic balancing  
   • Static load balancing – The charging power of each EVSE (electric-vehicle supply equipment) is capped at a fixed share of the total available capacity. For example, if your supply can provide 40 A and you have two chargers, each may be limited to 20 A regardless of whether both sockets are in use.  
   • Dynamic load balancing – Real-time monitoring of total load (via internal meters or an energy-management system) continuously adjusts each charger’s output. If one vehicle finishes charging or reduces its draw, the freed-up power is automatically reallocated to any other connected EV.  

3. Local vs. Centralized control  
   • Local (decentralized) systems – Chargers communicate peer-to-peer (usually via a simple bus like Modbus or PLC). They negotiate their share of the available current without an external server.  
   • Centralized systems – A master controller or cloud-based management platform polls all chargers, meters total building load, and issues set-point commands to each charger via a protocol such as OCPP (Open Charge Point Protocol).  

4. Integration with broader energy management  
   • Renewable integration – Load balancing systems can be linked to on-site solar or wind generation. When surplus renewable power is available, charging can be boosted; when onsite generation drops, charging is throttled back.  
   • Time-of-use or demand-response signals – Chargers can adjust power levels automatically in response to utility price signals or grid-operator requests, further smoothing peaks and lowering energy costs.  

5. Benefits in practice  
   • Scalability – You can start with a small supply and add more charging points over time, confident the management system will distribute power safely.  
   • User experience – Drivers experience consistent, reliable charging—even if full power isn’t always available, they can still top up at a sensible rate.  
   • Future-proofing – As battery capacities grow and fast-charging becomes more common, smart load balancing ensures you’re ready without repeated hardware upgrades.  

In short, load balancing is the intelligence layer that lets multiple EV chargers share a limited power supply fairly and efficiently, protecting both your electrical installation and your wallet while maximizing the uptime and speed of EV charging.

In Sweden there are several national and local programmes that can help finance or subsidize apartment-building insulation measures. Which schemes you can access will depend on whether you live in a tenant-owner association, condominiums (bostadsrättsförening) or a rental property, and on your municipality’s own offerings. Below is a summary of the most commonly used grants and subsidies:

1. ROT-avdrag (Tax Deduction for Renovation)  
   • What it is: A 30 percent tax credit on labour costs for repair, maintenance and energy-saving improvements.   
   • Eligible measures: Insulation of exterior walls, roofs, crawl-spaces, attic floors, etc., provided the work is performed by a registered contractor.  
   • Limits: Maximum SEK 50 000 per person per year (labour cost only). The building owner (e.g. your bostadsrättsförening) must administer the deduction.  

2. Enovas stöd för flerbostadshus (Energy Agency Grants for Multi-dwelling Buildings)  
   • What it is: Grants administered by the Swedish Energy Agency (Energimyndigheten) to improve energy performance in apartment blocks.  
   • Eligible measures: Thermal-envelope upgrades (façade, roof, floor insulation), new ventilation units with heat recovery, window replacement and more.

   • What it is: A joint national-local programme run by the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency (Naturvårdsverket) with funding channeled through regional and municipal offices.  
   • Eligible measures: High-impact energy savings such as extensive façade or roof insulation, coupled heat-pump and solar-thermal solutions, etc.  
   • Grant level: Often covers 50–80 percent of eligible costs, depending on the project’s climate benefit.  
   • How to apply: Each county administrative board (länsstyrelse) and many municipalities open calls several times a year. You must submit a project description with quantified CO₂ savings.

   • Many Swedish municipalities and regions run their own eco-investment funds or “värmebidrag” for smaller energy-saving upgrades.  
   • Conditions, application windows and grant levels vary widely – check your local kommun’s website under “energi, miljö & klimat.”  

5. EU-funded or Special Programmes  
   • In some larger renovation projects, it may be possible to tap EU regional development funds or national programmes aimed at sustainable urban development.  
   • These tend to have stricter eligibility requirements and longer lead times.  

Tips for a successful application  
- Start with an energy audit: An accredited energy consultant will identify the most cost-effective insulation measures and calculate expected energy savings.  
- Pool resources in your association: For condominiums, the förening (association) must be the applicant. A unanimous decision at a föreningsstämma is usually required.  
- Plan well in advance: Both Enova and Klimatklivet have limited budgets and specific application rounds.  
- Document everything: You’ll need quotes from certified contractors, before-and-after U-value calculations, and proof of payment.

By combining ROT deductions with Enova- or Klimatklivet-funded grants – plus any local eco-funds – it is often possible to cover a large share of the cost for major insulation projects in apartment buildings. Begin by contacting an energy-audit firm or your municipality’s energy advisor to map out the best route for your specific building.

   • Target – All private homeowners and apartment associations (housing companies) who carry out renovation, conversion or extension work.  
   • Measures – Among other things, replacement of windows and doors, installation of heat pumps, ventilation systems, heat recovery units, etc.  
   • Benefit – 30 percent deduction on the labour cost (maximum deduction SEK 50 000 per person per year for ROT), directly applied on the invoice. No support for materials.  
   • Note – You engage an approved contractor who handles the deduction in the invoice.  

3. Klimatklivet (“The Climate Leap”)  
   • Target – Municipalities, county councils, companies and other organisations with larger climate-saving investment projects.  
   • Measures – Industrial heat recovery, biofuel boilers, electric buses, large-scale energy efficiency upgrades, etc.  
   • Support level – Varies on the project’s CO₂‐reduction potential; can cover up to 50 percent of eligible investment costs.  
   • Application – Through the Swedish Environmental Protection Agency once a year (calls for proposals usually in spring).  

4. Boverket’s loan for energy-efficiency improvements  
   • Target – Multi-family dwellings owned by private individuals or housing companies; also small commercial properties.  
   • Measures – Thermal renovation, improved ventilation, new heating systems, etc.

5. Municipal and regional programmes  
   • Many municipalities and county administrative boards (Länsstyrelser) run local grants or loans to stimulate energy-saving investments.  
   • Examples – Small subsidies for attic or basement insulation; interest-free loans for heat pump installations; free or subsidised energy audits.

   • Target – Anyone installing photovoltaic (PV) systems on residential or commercial buildings.

Improving lighting in basement areas typically requires a combination of strategies that bring in as much daylight as possible, optimize artificial lighting, and ensure energy-efficient operation. Below are several approaches you can consider:

1. Introduce or enlarge daylight sources  
   • Light wells or sunken courtyards – excavate small courtyards or “light wells” at exterior walls, then install windows or glass doors down at basement level. This can bring in natural light and ventilation.  
   • Glass block windows – where security or privacy is an issue, glass‐block installations still admit diffuse daylight while maintaining insulation and sound control.  
   • Solar tubes or tubular daylight devices – these collect sunlight at roof level and channel it down through highly reflective tubes to ceiling fixtures in the basement.  

2. Select high-performance artificial fixtures  
   • LED technology – modern LEDs offer high luminous efficacy (often 100–150 lm/W), long life (50 000 h+), and good color rendering (CRI > 80), making them ideal for constant-use areas.  
   • Uniform, glare-controlled luminaires – flush-mount or recessed LED panels with diffusers help spread light evenly and minimize harsh shadows or glare on work surfaces.  
   • Task lighting – under-cabinet or adjustable wall-mounted fixtures in work areas (desks, laundry benches, hobby rooms) ensure the right amount of light exactly where it’s needed without over-illuminating the entire space.  

3. Layer and zone your lighting  
   • Ambient lighting – a network of evenly spaced ceiling fixtures provides base illumination (e.g. 150–300 lux for storage rooms, 300–500 lux for hobby or fitness areas).  
   • Accent or display lighting – directional spotlights highlight features, artwork or shelving. This breaks up the space visually and prevents a “cave-like” feel.  
   • Controls and zoning – divide the basement into circuits or zones with separate switches or dimmers so you only light the areas you’re using.  

4. Enhance reflectivity and light distribution  
   • Light-colored finishes – paint walls and ceilings in pale, matte or eggshell whites to maximize light reflection.  
   • Reflective flooring or large-format tile – glossy or semi-gloss surfaces help bounce light back into the space.  
   • Mirrors or translucent room dividers – strategically placed mirrors can redirect daylight or fixture light deeper into the basement.  

5. Incorporate smart controls and energy efficiency  
   • Occupancy/motion sensors – automatically turn lights on when someone enters and off when the space is unoccupied, reducing wasted energy.  
   • Daylight harvesting – in areas served by sun tunnels or windows, integrate sensors that dim electric lighting when sufficient daylight is available.  
   • Timers and programmable controls – schedule stairwell or hallway lighting to match typical usage patterns.  

6. Safety and compliance  
   • Emergency lighting – ensure exit paths and stairwells have backup luminaires or battery‐operated emergency fixtures per local building codes.  
   • Minimum illuminance levels – check applicable standards (e.g., 100 lux for general storage, 200 lux for laundry rooms, 300–500 lux for workshop areas) and verify with a light meter.  

By combining better access to daylight with a carefully designed LED‐based lighting layout, zoned controls and reflective finishes, you’ll transform a dark basement into a well-lit, energy-efficient and comfortable part of your building.

1. Commission an Energy Audit

   – Wall Insulation: External or internal wall insulation can reduce heat losses significantly, especially in older masonry or timber-frame constructions.  
   – Windows and Doors: Replace single-glazed frames with high-performance double or triple glazing. Ensure airtight seals around frames to eliminate drafts.

3. Improve Air Tightness and Ventilation  
   – Seal cracks around windows, doors, service penetrations and junctions between building elements.  
   – Install or upgrade mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR or FTX units) to ensure fresh air supply while retaining up to 90 % of outgoing heat.

4. Optimize Heating, Cooling and Domestic Hot Water Systems  
   – Replace old boilers or electric heaters with high-efficiency condensing boilers, heat pumps (ground‐source or air‐source) or district heating connections where available.  
   – Insulate hot‐water pipes and storage tanks to reduce distribution losses.  
   – Fit programmable or smart thermostats and implement zoning controls to avoid overheating or conditioning unoccupied areas.

5. Upgrade Lighting and Electrical Equipment  
   – Retrofit all lighting to LED technology. LEDs use 50–80 % less electricity than incandescent or fluorescent lamps.  
   – Install occupancy sensors and daylight dimmers in corridors, bathrooms and meeting rooms.  
   – When possible, choose ENERGY STAR or equivalent high‐efficiency appliances and office equipment.

6. Integrate Renewable Energy Sources  
   – Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels can offset a significant portion of your building’s electricity consumption.  
   – Consider solar thermal systems for domestic hot water pre-heating or small heat pumps.

   – Use a building management system (BMS) or sub-metering to monitor energy flows in real time.

   – Educate staff or tenants on simple measures: closing doors and windows when heating is on, turning off lights and equipment when not in use, and reporting faults promptly.  
   – Display energy dashboards or monthly performance reports to sustain awareness and drive behavior change.

By following these steps—starting with a professional energy audit and then systematically upgrading insulation, ventilation, technical systems and controls—you’ll target the largest energy losses first and ensure each investment delivers the highest possible return in both cost savings and carbon reduction.

Before moving forward with solar-PV on a multi-unit building, the board should carry out a systematic review in at least the following areas:

1. Regulatory and ownership rights  
   • Association statutes and house rules: Do they permit rooftop installations or require member approval?  
   • Zoning and detailed plans: Does the local municipality’s comprehensive plan or heritage‐protection status restrict alterations to the façade or roof?  
   • Building permit requirements: In many Swedish municipalities, mounting solar panels on existing roofs is permit‐exempt, but you should always confirm with the local byggnadsnämnd.  

2. Technical and structural feasibility  
   • Roof structure and load capacity: Ask a structural engineer to verify that the roof can carry the additional dead load (panels, mounting rails, ballast) and any imposed wind/uplift loads.  
   • Roof condition and remaining service life: If the shingles, membrane or waterproofing needs renewal within 5–7 years, it may make sense to reroof at the same time.  
   • Orientation, tilt and shading analysis: Use solar-simulation tools or on-site measurements to estimate annual yield given roof azimuth, pitch and shading from adjacent buildings or trees.  

3. Building services and electrical integration  
   • Main switchboard capacity and wiring routes: Ensure there is adequate space in the meter cabinet/central distribution board for a bidirectional meter and PV inverter connection.  
   • Metering and grid connection: Coordinate with your grid operator (elnätsföretag) on net-metering rules or export limitations.  
   • Fire and safety regulations: Confirm access requirements for emergency services and compliance with SS-EN roof-access standards.  

4. Energy performance and return on investment  
   • EPC (Energy Performance Certificate) review: Your latest epc_egienergiklass tells you the building’s current energy rating. Coupling solar generation with energy efficiency measures (e.g. improved insulation) can maximize savings.  
   • Financial analysis: Calculate investment cost, expected annual production (kWh), self-consumption rate, feed-in tariff and payback period. Investigate available subsidies or green loans.  

5. Insurance, warranties and maintenance  
   • Insurance coverage: Notify your property insurer and ensure the policy covers fire, storm and liability for installed PV panels.  
   • Warranties: Select panels and inverters with at least 10- to 20-year performance warranties and 5- to 10-year product warranties.  
   • Maintenance plan: Define responsibility for periodic inspections, roof cleaning and inverter service.  

6. Procurement and stakeholder communication  
   • Competitive tendering: Invite multiple qualified installers to submit turnkey proposals that include structural design, electrical works, documentation (e.g. K2/K3 checklist) and grid-operator liaison.  
   • Member information and decision process: Present findings, investment model and expected benefits at an ordinance-compliant meeting; secure any required vote or consent before proceeding.  

By systematically verifying each of these points—legal-administrative, technical, financial and organizational—you will minimize risks, ensure regulatory compliance and optimize long-term performance of your solar installation.

Ventilation balancing refers to the process of adjusting and fine-tuning the airflow rates in a building’s ventilation system so that each supply and exhaust outlet delivers the intended volume of air. Proper balancing ensures that the system is neither under- nor over-ventilating any zone, and it has several key implications for energy use:

1. Reduced Heat Losses and Gains  
   • When airflow rates match design values, conditioned (heated or cooled) air is delivered only where needed.  
   • Over-ventilation leads to unnecessary heating in winter or cooling in summer, driving up energy consumption.  
   • Under-ventilation can force occupants to open windows for fresh air, bypassing heat-recovery units or mechanical cooling and increasing thermal losses.

2. Improved Heat-Recovery Performance  
   • Many modern ventilation systems include heat- or energy-recovery units that transfer heat between the exhaust and supply air streams.  
   • If airflow is unbalanced, the heat exchanger cannot operate at its optimal effectiveness, reducing the recovered energy and increasing the net heating or cooling load.

3. Lower Fan and Pump Energy  
   • Imbalanced systems often result in higher duct pressures or unexpected leaks, forcing fans to work harder.  
   • Proper balancing minimizes pressure differences and duct losses, so fans can operate closer to their most efficient point on the performance curve.

4. Enhanced Indoor Air Quality with Less Energy  
   • Balanced systems ensure that stale air is removed and fresh air is supplied at the correct rate for occupant density and building usage.  
   • By avoiding over-ventilation, you supply only the necessary outdoor air, reducing the need to heat or cool excess ventilation air.

5. Longer Equipment Life and Reduced Maintenance  
   • When ventilation equipment operates under the correct loads, stresses on fans, motors and control components are minimized.  
   • This reduces maintenance needs, unexpected failures and the associated energy spikes during restart or repair.

In summary, ventilation balancing optimizes both thermal comfort and air quality while minimizing the energy required for heating, cooling and fan operation. Properly balanced systems—including those with heat-recovery ventilation—can cut overall HVAC energy use by 10–30 percent, depending on the building type and climate.

  • If the building has an exhaust-only system or natural ventilation, investigate installing a balanced mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR). Achieving 70–80 % heat recovery can reduce heating demand by up to 15 %.  
  • Commission airflow measurements and heat recovery efficiency tests to size the units correctly.  

4. Heating system upgrades  
  • Assess the existing heating plant: older oil or electric boilers, oversized district-heating substations or ineffective radiator sizing.  
  • Consider high-efficiency condensing boilers, district heating upgrades or, where feasible, a common ground-source or air-source heat pump solution.  
  • Install smart radiator thermostats and weather-compensation controls to optimize distribution.  

5. Renewable energy and controls  
  • Feasibility study for photovoltaic (PV) panels on the roof or south-facing façades; even a 20–50 kW system can cover a good share of common-area electricity.  
  • Solar-thermal collectors for domestic hot water pre-heating.  
  • Building energy management system (BEMS) or sub-metering in each stairwell to track consumption and pinpoint inefficiencies.  

6. Next steps  
  1. Order the latest EPC (energideklaration) to confirm the building’s current energy class (epc_egienergiklass) and review the official list of suggested measures.  
  2. Undertake an infrared survey (thermography) and blower-door test to quantify actual thermal bridges and air-leakage rates.  
  3. Prepare a package of measures sorted by cost vs. savings (simple payback / life-cycle cost) for the homeowner association to prioritize.  

By starting with the building envelope and ventilation—where the largest thermal losses typically occur—you’ll maximize your CO₂ savings and financial returns before moving on to more capital-intensive heating or renewable-energy investments.
